 Portable power stations are useful for everything from keeping your broadband running during a power cut to powering equipment away from a convenient socket. The Anker Solix S2000 fits both roles, combining a substantial battery with a relatively compact upright design.
 What impressed me most, though, was how little fuss it involved. It handled repeated sessions with a 1,200W wet/dry vacuum straight out of the box, while the accompanying app was easy to set up and refreshingly clear about what its settings actually do.

 Design and connections 
 The S2000 has an understated appearance: a dark grey enclosure, rounded edges and a glossy front panel. It looks perfectly at home beside a desk, although mine was soon earning its keep around DIY equipment.
 Its upright shape gives it a reasonably small footprint. At 16.2kg, however, “portable” still involves a deliberate lift. Moving it between rooms or taking it out to the garden is one thing; carrying it a long distance is another.
 The UK version has four proper Type G sockets, split evenly between the front and rear. That arrangement makes sense. You can keep regularly connected equipment plugged in behind the unit, leaving the front sockets available for things you connect occasionally.
 There is a trade-off: you’ll need access to both sides if you want to use every socket. Bear that in mind before squeezing it into a tight space, and leave the ventilation clear.

 The USB connections sit above the display. The 100W USB-C port is the one to choose for a compatible laptop, while the other USB-C connection is limited to 15W. They look similar, so it’s worth checking the labels.
 The screen puts the remaining battery percentage front and centre, alongside input and output wattage and an estimated remaining time. That gives you the information you need without reaching for your phone.
 Performance: a proper day’s work 
 My S2000 arrived with a 59% state of charge. Rather than charging it fully before doing anything useful, I put it straight to work powering a 1,200W wet/dry vacuum.
 Between approximately 10am and 5pm, I used the vacuum repeatedly in sessions lasting around five to ten minutes. The Anker handled those sessions without any problems, and by the time I finished, it still showed 13% remaining.
 To be clear, that was intermittent use across a seven-hour working day, rather than seven hours of continuous vacuuming. Even so, it was a useful practical test: repeated use of a fairly demanding appliance, starting with little more than half a battery.
 The benefit was simple. I could get on with the job without running an extension lead back to a mains socket, and the power station had enough charge to cover the work I needed to do.
 This wasn’t a controlled capacity test. I didn’t record the vacuum’s total running time or measure the energy delivered at the socket, so it wouldn’t be fair to calculate an efficiency figure from the percentage drop.
 What I can say is that it coped comfortably with this particular vacuum and pattern of use.
 The main limitation is the 1,500W continuous output. Battery capacity tells you how much energy is stored; output determines which appliances it can run. A large battery doesn’t automatically mean it can power a typical high-wattage UK kettle or several demanding tools together.
 Check appliance ratings, allow for starting demands, and remember that the output limit is shared across the AC sockets.
 Charging options 
 (Image credit: Future) For everyday charging, the S2000 connects directly to the mains using the supplied AC cable. There’s no separate external power brick to find space for.
 During one charging session, the front display showed approximately 1,068W going in. An app screenshot taken during charging showed around 1,077W, with UltraFast charging switched off. These are snapshots rather than a timed charging test, but they show a substantial charging rate in normal use.
 There’s also an app-controlled UltraFast option when a quicker turnaround matters.
 Away from home, the S2000 supports compatible solar panels and vehicle charging, provided you have the correct cables and accessories. Solar input is capped at 400W, with Anker specifying a maximum open-circuit voltage of 60V. Panel compatibility matters as well as the connector.
 Those alternatives add flexibility, although a normal car accessory socket will be much slower than mains charging. Think of it as a way to replenish charge while travelling, rather than expecting a quick refill of a 2kWh battery.
 The app: easy to set up, easy to understand 
 (Image credit: Future || Anker) The app was one of the nicest surprises.
 Finding it in the Google Play Store was straightforward, as were signing in and getting started. The S2000 was detected straight away, added without difficulty and ready to control. An iPhone version also appears to be available, although my experience here was with Android.
 The main screen presents the battery percentage, temperature, charging estimate and power flow clearly. You can see what’s happening at a glance.
 More useful still is the depth of control. There are multiple UPS and power-management modes, charging timers, adjustable AC charging power and battery charge limits. You also get AC output scheduling, a countdown to switch the sockets off, screen controls and power-usage history.
 Crucially, the explanations are good. Rather than leaving you to decipher a vaguely named mode, the app helps you understand what a setting does and decide whether it suits your needs.
 Some power-station apps make configuration feel like educated guesswork. Here, the guidance makes the extra features more approachable, particularly if this is your first battery system.
 Backup power and everyday use 
 The UPS function adds another potential role: keeping suitable equipment powered when the mains fails. Anker quotes a transfer time of around 10ms, although I haven’t independently measured that or tested compatibility with individual computers.
 For a home office, the combination of rear sockets, battery monitoring and configurable operating modes is appealing. You can leave equipment connected and manage the unit without constantly handling it.

 A winter outage is a terrible time to discover that your big battery reboots the router—or that your NAS has no idea the battery is nearly empty. Buy for transfer time, runtime and shutdown communication , in that order. A bigger watt-hour number solves only the middle one.
 Specifications and transfer times below come from the makers and NUT project; runtime examples are calculated assumptions.
 Quick picks: which battery fits your job?
 Best UPS-mode power station: EcoFlow RIVER 3 Max. Its RIVER 3 Plus base has a maker-rated under-10 ms transfer and a USB-B communication port. The 572 Wh package adds an EB300 battery. It is the strongest fit here for networking plus a computer or NAS, with a shutdown test as part of setup.
 Best for a router only: EcoFlow RIVER 3 230Wh. You get ordinary AC output in a smaller battery package. Its maker specifies transfer within 20 ms ; run a power-loss test with your router before relying on it. EcoFlow explicitly excludes NAS and other uninterrupted computer loads from this version’s intended use.
 Best capacity: BLUETTI AC180. Its 1,152 Wh battery is the largest here. Choose it when longer runtime matters and your equipment tolerates its 20 ms transfer with Grid Enhancement off ; its AC inverter’s own consumption matters at router-sized loads.
 For portable DC devices: Anker SOLIX C300 DC. This is a 288 Wh DC-only battery, with no AC outlets and no published UPS transfer figure in the maker guide we checked. Buy it for compatible USB/DC devices, not as a drop-in NAS UPS.
 For a NAS-first purchase where orderly shutdown is the main goal, also read our small-rack UPS buying guide . A conventional UPS can be the better tool even when its battery is smaller.

 The EcoFlow US series page separates Max from Plus and Max Plus. Max is 286 Wh + 286 Wh = 572 Wh ; Max Plus is a different package. The RIVER 3 manual also separates the 230Wh model from a distinct 10 ms UPS version. Pick by the full model name.
 Use continuous output ratings for electronics. EcoFlow’s X-Boost heating-appliance claims and BLUETTI’s lifting-mode headline are not extra normal AC capacity for your NAS.
 Will UPS mode switch fast enough?
 Pass-through means the station can supply a load while connected to input power. Transfer time tells you how long the interruption is when that input disappears. Those are different buying questions.
 The RIVER 3 Max has the best published transfer figure among these AC candidates. EcoFlow’s Plus manual describes the base unit as a standby UPS with transfer within 10 ms; its US page advertises under 10 ms. Choose it first for the UPS-mode job, then test the actual equipment.
 For comparison, the line-interactive CyberPower CP1500PFCLCDa has a maker-listed typical 4 ms transfer, automatic voltage regulation and USB management. “Typical” and a maximum-style claim are different specifications, so don’t turn those numbers into an exact speed ratio. Our NAS UPS buying guide covers pure versus stepped sine, USB/NUT evidence and setup for TrueNAS, Unraid and Synology; the CyberPower specifications explain the conventional UPS option.
 A router’s power brick may ride through a short gap, but the way to find out is a controlled transfer test. A NAS also needs time to stop writes and shut down. That makes communication just as important as fast switching.
 Skip RIVER 3 230 for a NAS. Its manual specifically tells you not to connect NAS servers, desktops and similar devices requiring uninterrupted supply. Its 20 ms EPS feature is useful for suitable loads; it does not make it the same product as the Plus/Max.
 How long will your router, ONT and NAS run?
 Start with a plug-in power meter , not the power brick’s maximum label. Measure the equipment together, including any switch needed to keep it useful. For a NAS, include a busy period and drive startup in your output-capacity check.
 Here is a planning worksheet with deliberately stated inputs:
 Router plus modem: 20 W combined .
 Add an optical network terminal, or ONT: 10 W , taking the total to 30 W . Include this only if your connection actually uses one alongside those devices.
 Add a mini PC: 20 W , taking the total to 50 W .
 Add a two-bay NAS: 30 W , taking the total to 80 W .
 These are assumed loads, not typical-use measurements. For every AC example, assume 90% usable battery, 85% inverter efficiency and 15 W fixed station overhead . The AC180 manual uses this calculation structure, quotes about 15 W self-consumption and gives 90% depth of discharge with inverter efficiency above 85%. Applying those same values to EcoFlow is a comparison assumption, not an EcoFlow efficiency specification.
 Hours = nominal Wh × 0.90 × 0.85 ÷ (load W + 15 W)

 The low-load trap is worth seeing: ignoring fixed overhead gives the AC180 44.1 hours at the assumed 20 W load; including the manual’s approximately 15 W consumption gives 25.2 hours . That is why “battery Wh divided by router watts” is too optimistic.
 For a long outage, shut down the mini PC and NAS once their work is safe and leave the network running. Also remember that keeping your modem powered does not keep the provider’s upstream equipment powered.
 Can it tell NUT to shut down your NAS?
 RIVER 3 Max is the exception worth knowing about. Its Plus base has a USB-B data port, and EcoFlow documents Power Manager software for PC/NAS monitoring and automatic shutdown. Separately, NUT’s hardware compatibility list lists RIVER 3 Plus over USB with usbhid-ups .
 That gives you a documented route to explore, rather than a charge-only USB socket. Use a NUT package that includes the model’s support, connect the data cable and verify that the host sees mains loss, battery state and the shutdown event. A NAS appliance’s bundled NUT version and device list can differ from the current project list.
 The AC180, RIVER 3 230 and C300 DC manuals checked here do not document a USB UPS management interface. Their USB charging sockets cannot supply a battery-status signal simply because a cable fits. If automatic NAS shutdown is your priority, choose the Max’s supported communication route or a conventional managed UPS.
 Our UPS sizing and graceful-shutdown guide walks through the complete dependency chain: the protected host, the controller and any networking needed to deliver the shutdown command. A battery can keep supplying power long after a host has lost the network path it needs.
 Where the C300 DC makes sense
 The Anker A1726 guide lists USB-C outputs and a 12 V, 10 A car socket. It suits compatible portable devices, including USB-C equipment that accepts the offered power profile. It does not accept a router’s AC power brick.
 For a barrel-powered router, voltage, connector, polarity and current all have to match through a suitable regulated power arrangement. Don’t turn this purchase into an improvised cable project. An AC-output station lets you retain the equipment’s original power adapters instead.
 The maker guide publishes no UPS switchover figure or seamless pass-through commitment for this DC model. It also documents low-current USB auto-off behavior after two hours. Choose it as portable backup, and choose one of the AC UPS-mode options when automatic changeover is the job.
 Set it up before the first storm
 For off-grid texts, choose a battery-powered Meshtastic starter node and test messages with a second node before the next outage.
 Choose the protected load. Keep the list short: internet equipment first, then a host or NAS with a clear shutdown job. Measure watts and use the sizing guide for W/VA headroom.
 Give the station ventilation. Follow its manual’s placement and charging instructions; keep intake and exhaust clear.
 Set UPS and low-load options. On AC180, turn Grid Enhancement off in the BLUETTI app: the manual’s page 13 says it lengthens switchover when enabled. Disable AC ECO auto-off for an always-on small load too. On EcoFlow RIVER 3 230 and the Plus base in Max, set AC timeout to Never in the EcoFlow app so an idle outlet stays on.
 Connect shutdown data where supported. On Max, use the Plus base’s USB-B communication port, then configure and verify the software on the actual protected host.
 Test a mains failure. Follow the maker’s outage-test procedure with nonessential workloads first. Watch whether the router reboots, the host reports battery operation and the NAS completes an orderly shutdown with charge remaining.
 Test recovery too. Restore input power and observe charging, outlet state and host restart behavior. Write down what needs a button press so the next outage has fewer surprises.
 Buy RIVER 3 Max for the most complete UPS-mode package here, RIVER 3 230 for suitable router-only duty, or AC180 for the larger energy reserve. Keep C300 DC on the portable-DC shortlist. For a NAS whose main job is surviving a brief interruption and shutting down cleanly, start with the conventional UPS guide and let the shutdown plan decide.

 Quick Answer 
 A portable power station with official UPS or EPS behavior can help some home servers, NAS drives, and network gear through a brief outage, but only when the transfer time, outlet, and power limits fit the connected device. A 10 ms or 20 ms transfer is fast, but it is not 0 ms. If the device manual calls for 0 ms transfer, continuous voltage and frequency regulation, standard UPS communication, or a critical SLA, an online double-conversion UPS is the safer choice.
 Use a PPS when the device manual accepts the model's published transfer time and the load stays within the correct UPS outlet or bypass limit.
 Use an online UPS when the load needs 0 ms transfer, continuous voltage and frequency regulation, UPS communication, or a critical service-level agreement (SLA).
 A home server setup rarely starts with a full backup plan. It may begin with one small server under a desk, then a NAS, an ONT, a router, a switch, and a Wi-Fi AP sharing the same corner. Most days, that setup feels settled. A short power dip can still expose one weak point: one device restarts, storage needs time to close cleanly, and the network path may be the only way to send an alert. Before adding more battery capacity, check the power behavior first.

 Pass-through charging tells you the energy path: the unit can receive input power while it supplies output power under stated conditions. For a home server or NAS, that is only one part of the decision.
 Before connecting storage or server equipment, check the UPS transfer time, supported outlet, input condition, and output limit for the exact model and outlet you plan to use. The device manual matters too. If the server PSU, NAS, or network adapter only allows 0 ms transfer, choose an online UPS for that load.
 Why 10ms or 20ms is not 0ms
 A 10 ms or 20 ms switchover may be enough for some electronics, but the protected device makes the final call. Server power supplies, NAS adapters, and small network power bricks can respond differently during the same voltage dip.
 We recommend checking the equipment manual before relying on a portable power station as UPS protection. If the server, NAS, router, or switch manual does not allow the listed transfer time, move that load to an online UPS. A portable power station can still help with longer runtime for equipment that does not need 0 ms transfer.
 Build a Whole-Room Load Inventory
 A whole-room backup plan works best when the device list comes before the battery size. Start with the equipment that keeps data, internet access, and alerts working, then match the power station to that load. If possible, measure each device with a plug-in watt meter or smart PDU. Published specs and adapter labels are helpful starting points, but servers, hard drives, and PoE switches can draw more power during boot, backups, drive spin-up, or heavier network activity.

 Once the table is filled in, add up only the devices that must stay online during backup mode. Compare that running load with the official continuous output limit for the outlet group you plan to use. Leave room for startup peaks, future equipment, and warmer operating conditions so the setup is not sized too close to the edge.
 Next, narrow the list to what truly protects data and access. A core server, NAS, router, ONT, or necessary switch may need backup power, depending on your setup. A monitor, printer, nonessential external drive, or noncritical PoE device can often stay off during an outage. The goal is to keep the right devices online, not every device in the room.

 When you compare Anker SOLIX models for a server or NAS, start with the outlet you plan to use. Capacity matters, but the safer choice also depends on transfer time, input condition, and the bypass limit for that outlet.  How to Estimate Runtime for a Server and NAS
 Runtime is easier to estimate after you measure the load. If you have a full-day energy reading for the server, NAS, and network gear you want to keep online, use this formula:
 Runtime = Capacity (kWh) × Inverter Efficiency ÷ Daily Energy Use (kWh / Day)
 Use the inverter-efficiency value listed for the exact model and use case you are calculating. If you only have nominal capacity, and the model does not list usable capacity for your setup, treat the result as a theoretical estimate rather than a guaranteed runtime.
 For a steadier server-room load, you can also convert watts to kilowatts and estimate runtime in hours: capacity in kWh × model-specific inverter efficiency ÷ load in kW. Keep extra margin for battery reserve settings and heavier jobs, such as backups, drive rebuilds, or higher network activity.
 Can a Portable Power Station Automatically Shut Down a NAS?
 A portable power station can keep AC power available, but automatic NAS shutdown needs a separate UPS status signal. That signal matters because a NAS may be writing files, syncing data, or rebuilding an array when power drops. A clean shutdown gives storage time to stop services and close properly, instead of coming back to file-system checks, failed jobs, or a rebuild you did not plan for.
 Power Backup and UPS Communication Are Different Features
 When you see UPS transfer time listed, read it as outlet power behavior. It does not mean the station can send a USB, SNMP, or network UPS event to a NAS. For unattended storage, add automatic shutdown only when the power station instructions and the NAS compatibility list show the same supported communication path. If you cannot find that match, use a communication-capable UPS for the shutdown signal and keep the portable power station focused on backup runtime.
 What Your NAS Needs for Automatic Shutdown
 Before relying on automatic shutdown, check the NAS brand, model, and system version against the NAS maker’s UPS documentation. Synology, QNAP, and TrueNAS systems can support UPS-based shutdown, but the supported method depends on the model, system version, and UPS communication path. Look for a supported USB UPS, SNMP UPS, or network UPS tools setup such as NUT.
 USB charging ports and app monitoring are not UPS communication. The NAS needs a UPS status signal it can read. If the NAS cannot receive that signal from the power source, protect storage with a compatible UPS and use the portable power station for loads that mainly need longer backup time.
 Can a Portable Power Station Stay Plugged In as a UPS 24/7?
 For a server or NAS, treat 24/7 plugged-in use as a model-specific decision. If the official instructions for your exact model clearly say it can stay connected to wall power in the mode you plan to use, follow those stated conditions. If they do not, check with Anker SOLIX Support before leaving it connected full time. Continuous AC input, pass-through charging, and bypass output describe how power moves. They should not be used by themselves as permission for 24/7 UPS use.
 When Do You Need an Online UPS Instead?
 Choose a purpose-built online UPS or another approved power system when the protected load needs stricter power behavior than a portable power station is built to provide.
 The equipment requires 0 ms transfer.
 The system needs continuous voltage or frequency regulation.
 The NAS or server must receive compatible UPS communication for automatic shutdown.
 The load, startup peak, input condition, or outlet use exceeds the portable power station’s official limits.
 A service target or system design requires online double-conversion UPS.
 The portable power station information for your model does not confirm the needed port, long-term connection, or use case.
 For medical, life-safety, or other regulated applications, use only a power system approved by the equipment manufacturer and applicable regulations. Do not describe a standard portable power station as approved for these applications unless official documentation explicitly confirms it.
 Conclusion
 A safer backup plan starts with the device that is hardest to interrupt. Measure the server, NAS, router, ONT, switch, Wi-Fi AP, and external drives that must stay online, then compare the device manual with the power station’s transfer time, outlet behavior, and output limit. Before choosing a model, confirm whether the NAS can receive a supported UPS status signal for automatic shutdown. If one of those checks fails, move the sensitive load to an online UPS and use portable backup power for devices that mainly need longer runtime. After an outage, bring sensitive equipment back carefully. Ready.gov recommends that users protect electronics from power-return surges when power returns.
 FAQ
 Is a 10ms UPS switchover the same as zero downtime?
 No. A 10 ms switchover is a limited transfer time, not 0 ms transfer. Whether the device stays online depends on its hold-up time and how the exact setup behaves during testing. If your server PSU, NAS adapter, or network gear cannot ride through that gap, choose an online double-conversion UPS for that load.
 Can a portable power station back up a home server and NAS?
 Yes, for some setups. A portable power station can be considered when transfer time, continuous and peak load, outlet condition, input condition, and 24/7 use all match the official requirements for the model and the connected device. For critical server or storage loads, an online UPS is the safer starting point.
 Is pass-through charging the same as UPS mode?
 No. Pass-through charging means the unit can accept input power while supplying output power under stated conditions. For UPS use, check the exact model and outlet for transfer behavior, transfer time, and output limit before connecting a server or NAS.
 When should I choose an online UPS instead of a portable power station?
 Choose an online UPS when the load needs 0 ms transfer, voltage and frequency regulation, standard UPS communication, critical database protection, a verifiable SLA, or when the equipment manual does not allow 10 ms or 20 ms transfer. For home setups where budget and flexibility matter, the   best portable power station   can fill the gap between a full UPS and basic backup, offering longer runtime and solar recharge at the cost of a slightly slower transfer time.

 How to Choose a Portable Power Station With UPS Mode in 2026
 Picking the right portable power station with UPS mode comes down to three numbers: switchover time in milliseconds, capacity in watt-hours, and what you actually need to keep running. Everything else is convenience.
 Switchover Time Thresholds: 10ms vs 20ms vs 30ms
 Switchover time is the single most important spec on this category. It is the gap between when grid power disappears and when the battery takes over. Anything you plug in must survive that gap using its own internal capacitance. Most desktop PSUs only hold up for 16 to 25 milliseconds. That means:
 Sub-10ms (verified NAS-compliant UPS): Keeps desktop towers, workstations, and NAS arrays alive without rebooting. Only a handful of portable power stations actually deliver this, including the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic, and the BLUETTI Elite units in this guide.
 10ms to 20ms: Works for routers, modems, laptops with internal batteries, and most home office gear. The OUPES Mega 1 lives here.
 20ms to 30ms (technically EPS, not UPS): Often marketed as “UPS mode” but really an Emergency Power Supply. Survives a flicker on a refrigerator or CPAP, but a sensitive desktop may reboot. EcoFlow’s older Delta Pro units fall here on certain firmware.
 If you want true NAS-compliant UPS performance in a portable form factor, only the sub-10ms units on this list qualify.
 Sizing Capacity to Your Load
 Use this rule of thumb: usable watt-hours equals total watt-hours times 0.85 (accounting for inverter losses and depth-of-discharge protection). Divide by your load wattage to estimate runtime.
 For a typical home setup, here is what I see in real testing:
 Wi-Fi 6 router + cable modem (15W): A 1024Wh unit runs roughly 58 hours. A 288Wh unit runs about 16 hours.
 Laptop (45W average): Roughly 19 hours on a 1024Wh unit, 5.4 hours on a 288Wh unit.
 CPAP without humidifier (35W): About 25 hours on 1024Wh, 7 hours on 288Wh.
 CPAP with humidifier + heated tubing (60W): Drops to roughly 14 hours on 1024Wh, 4 hours on 288Wh. CPAP users should oversize their unit.
 Desktop tower (180W): Roughly 4.8 hours on 1024Wh. Larger workstations need a 2kWh+ unit or expansion batteries.
 Starlink (40W average): About 21 hours on 1024Wh. Many users report higher 30 to 50W draws in real conditions.
 Dedicated UPS vs Portable Power Station vs Both
 This is the most important decision after switchover time. A traditional double-conversion online UPS has effectively 0ms transfer time, but it caps out at a few hundred watt-hours. A portable power station has minutes of transfer time and kilowatt-hours of capacity. Here is how I frame it:
 Pick a dedicated UPS if: You have a single tower, a NAS, and zero tolerance for reboots. The 0ms switchover is unmatched, and the runtime is enough for a graceful shutdown.
 Pick a portable power station if: You want multi-hour runtime, mobile use, and the ability to back up multiple devices through one unit.
 Pair both: For full home labs or critical NAS arrays, run the desktop and NAS off a 1500VA online UPS, then plug that UPS into the portable power station. You get instant switchover from the UPS and hours of runtime from the battery.
 Reviewers on Reddit’s r/homelab strongly recommend pairing both for serious home labs. The APC SMT1500 or CyberPower PR1500LCD paired with a 2kWh portable power station is the gold-standard setup for many technicians.
 The Eco-Mode Trap
 Several portable power stations include an “eco mode” or AC idle timeout that turns off the AC output after a few minutes of low draw. That is great for camping because it saves battery, but it kills UPS protection for a router drawing 12W. If your unit drops the AC output at 10 minutes of idle, your network dies during the first extended brownout.
 Before relying on any UPS-mode power station for a router, disable eco mode in the app. The Anker, EcoFlow, and BLUETTI units in this guide all let you do this in their respective apps.
 Battery Chemistry, Cycles, and 24/7 Use
 Every unit in this roundup uses LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) cells, which last 3000 to 4000 cycles before hitting 80% capacity. NMC cells in older units are cheaper but only last 500 to 1000 cycles.
 Leaving a portable power station plugged in 24/7 is generally fine with LiFePO4, but heat is the enemy. In a closet or attic with poor ventilation, the battery management system will throttle charging and the unit will not reach 100%. Place it in a cool spot with at least six inches of clearance on all sides. Fan noise at idle is another consideration; the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2’s silent mode and the Anker app’s “quiet hours” address this.
 Solar Input and Off-Grid Recharging
 Solar input determines how fast you can refill during a multi-day outage. The BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 leads at 1000W. The Anker SOLIX F3000 reaches 2400W with high-voltage panels. Most 1kWh units top out at 500 to 600W, which gives you a full recharge in roughly 2 to 3 hours of good sun. Cloud cover drops real-world output by 40 to 60%, so oversize your panel array.
 Brand Reliability: EcoFlow vs BLUETTI vs Anker vs OUPES
 Anker and EcoFlow have the longest track records and the broadest service networks in North America. BLUETTI is competitive on hardware but warranty enforcement for non-direct purchases is hit-or-miss. OUPES is newer but delivers strong value; expect support to take longer than the major brands.
 Testing Your UPS Setup
 Do not trust the marketing claim. Test it. Pull the wall plug while a sensitive load is running and watch what happens. A laptop will usually survive any switchover. A desktop tower or NAS is the real test. Run the test with a Kill-A-Watt or UPS monitoring software to log the event and check the transfer time. EcoFlow and Anker apps log UPS events automatically.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is UPS mode on a portable power station?
 UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) mode on a portable power station means the unit stays plugged into wall power, passes that grid power through to your devices, and automatically switches to battery backup within milliseconds when the grid fails. Sub-10ms switchover protects desktop PCs and NAS arrays. 10 to 20ms works for routers and laptops. Anything marketed as 20ms+ is technically EPS (Emergency Power Supply), not true UPS.
 Can a portable power station replace a dedicated UPS?
 Yes for short outages and casual use, but not for everyone. A sub-10ms portable power station with at least 1024Wh of capacity will outlast a typical 1500VA UPS by a wide margin on runtime. For zero-tolerance NAS or workstation protection, pair a double-conversion online UPS (APC SMT1500, CyberPower PR1500LCD) with a portable power station for both instant switchover and extended runtime.
 Does BLUETTI have UPS mode?
 Yes. BLUETTI’s Elite 30 V2 and Elite 100 V2 both deliver 10ms UPS switchover, which protects home servers, routers, and CPAP machines. Older BLUETTI units like the AC180 are rated around 20ms, which is technically EPS. The newer BLUETTI Apex 300 claims 0ms switchover for home lab use.
 Which is better for my PC, a UPS or a portable power station?
 For pure switchover safety, a dedicated double-conversion online UPS wins because it has effectively 0ms transfer time. A sub-10ms portable power station is the next best thing and lasts hours instead of minutes. For most home office and gaming PC users, a sub-10ms portable power station like the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 or EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic is enough. For critical NAS or server arrays, pair a dedicated UPS with a portable power station.
 What are the downsides of using a portable power station as a UPS?
 The biggest downsides are switchover speed (most units deliver 20ms+, which is technically EPS not UPS), eco-mode behavior (some units shut off low-wattage router loads during idle), 24/7 heat and fan noise (continuous operation generates heat and cycles the cooling fan), recovery after full discharge (some units fail to resume UPS function after hitting 0%), and warranty support for units left plugged in continuously. Verify your specific model supports continuous UPS duty before deploying.
 How long will a 1500VA UPS last?
 A 1500VA UPS at half load (about 450W) typically lasts 5 to 10 minutes. At quarter load (225W) it extends to 15 to 25 minutes. That is enough for a graceful shutdown but not for sustained work. A 1024Wh portable power station on the same 225W load runs about 3.5 to 4 hours. The portable power station wins on runtime; the dedicated UPS wins on switchover speed. Many home users pair both.
 Final Verdict: Which UPS Power Station Should You Buy in 2026?
 If you want one portable power station with UPS mode that handles a router, a desktop tower, a NAS, and a weekend of camping, the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 is still the unit I recommend. It earned the Editor’s Choice spot because it pairs the highest review count of any sub-10ms portable power station at this capacity with consistently clean switchover in my testing.
 If you want something lighter and cheaper, the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 is the pick. At 9.4 pounds and 10ms UPS, it is the most portable option on this list and is the easiest to deploy next to a home network rack. If you need to back up a single workstation, the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic is the smartest choice for app-driven automation and storm alerts. If your needs are bigger, the Anker SOLIX F3000 is the only unit in this group that approaches whole-home capability. For expandability up to 5kWh without buying a second unit, the OUPES Mega 1 is the value pick.
 Whichever you choose, disable eco mode before deploying as a UPS for a router, test the switchover by pulling the wall plug, and size your capacity to the load you actually need to keep running through an outage. The right portable power station with UPS mode will keep your devices alive through more than just a flicker.

 UPS Portable Power Station: Is It Possible?
 08/10/2026 | Anker 
 Blog Center 
 All 
 A power cut can interrupt a video call, corrupt files, disconnect your security system or switch off a freezer at the worst possible moment. A traditional UPS is designed to prevent that, but modern battery power stations now offer much larger capacities, solar charging and several useful outputs. So, can a portable power station replace a UPS?
 In this guide, we explain how a UPS portable power station works, what its limitations are and which specifications matter. You will learn when portable power station UPS mode is suitable for a PC, router, NAS or other equipment, and when a conventional UPS remains the safer choice.
 Table of contents
 Quick Answer 
 What Is a Portable Power Station UPS? 
 How Portable Power Station UPS Mode Works 
 What Should You Check Before Buying a Portable Power Station UPS?

 FAQ 
 Quick Answer
 Yes, you can use a portable power station as a UPS if the model specifically supports UPS, EPS or automatic backup mode. It must provide pass-through charging, a suitable transfer time, enough continuous output and a pure sine wave inverter. However, not every power station changes over quickly enough for every computer, server or medical device.
 What Is a Portable Power Station UPS?
 A portable power station UPS combines a rechargeable battery system with automatic backup functionality. To understand the difference, it helps to separate the everyday roles of a traditional UPS and a portable power station.
 How a Traditional UPS Works
 A traditional UPS sits between the mains socket and your equipment. It offers surge protection, charges its internal battery and changes to battery power automatically when the electricity fails. Standby models switch over during an outage, line-interactive models also regulate voltage, while online UPS systems continuously use the inverter.
 Most conventional UPS units are built for short outages, usually giving a computer enough time to save work and shut down safely. They are generally stationary, have modest capacity and may include USB communication for automatic shutdown software.
 How a Portable Power Station Works
 A portable power station stores energy in a lithium-ion or LiFePO4 battery, then uses an inverter to provide AC electricity. It may also include USB, USB-C, 12V and other DC outputs.
 You can normally recharge it from a mains socket, compatible solar panels or a vehicle. Capacity is measured in watt-hours (Wh), while continuous wattage shows the load it can run constantly. Surge wattage covers brief starting demands from motors and compressors.
 How Portable Power Station UPS Mode Works
 In UPS mode, mains electricity enters the power station and is passed through to your connected equipment. The internal battery remains ready, then the inverter takes over when the mains supply fails.
 Mains Pass-Through Operation
 With pass-through charging enabled, the wall socket supplies the station while your devices use its AC outputs. The battery stays charged or charges in the background. During a power cut, the station disconnects from the mains and begins producing inverter power.
 This arrangement is often called a portable power station UPS, EPS mode or backup mode, depending on the manufacturer. The names differ, so check the manual rather than relying on a marketing label alone.
 Transfer Time and Device Compatibility
 Transfer time is the brief gap between mains failure and battery output starting. Many power stations quote figures around 10–20 milliseconds, but the exact result depends on the model and the equipment connected.
 Most laptops tolerate this interruption because their internal battery continues operating. Desktop PCs, monitors and some networking hardware may also cope, but sensitive servers, storage systems or specialist equipment should be tested. A true online UPS provides continuous inverter power and removes this changeover concern.
 Pure Sine Wave Output
 Pure sine wave output closely matches the electricity supplied by the UK mains grid. It is preferable for desktop computers, monitors, audio equipment, medical electronics and motor-driven appliances such as fridges or pumps.
 Simulated or modified sine wave output can cause buzzing, extra heat, unreliable operation or compatibility problems with some power supplies and motors. If you plan to use a portable power station as a UPS, pure sine wave AC output is the sensible minimum for sensitive equipment.
 What Should You Check Before Buying a Portable Power Station UPS?
 Treat this as a practical buying checklist, not a general product recommendation. Compare the manufacturer’ s specifications with your actual equipment load, expected outage length and need for unattended shutdown.
 Explicit UPS, EPS or backup-mode support: Confirm that the feature is designed for automatic battery backup, not merely ordinary pass-through charging.
 Transfer time: Look for the published changeover time and check whether it is suitable for your PC, NAS or other equipment.
 Pure sine wave inverter: Choose pure sine wave output for sensitive electronics and motor-driven appliances.
 Continuous AC output: Add the running wattage of everything connected and leave a comfortable margin below the rated output.
 Surge or starting-wattage capability: Fridges, pumps and power tools can briefly demand much more than their normal running wattage.
 Usable watt-hour capacity: Battery ratings are not the same as energy delivered to AC equipment. Allow for inverter losses and avoid planning around every advertised Wh.
 Pass-through charging: The station must be able to power equipment while charging from mains without disabling the AC output.
 LiFePO4 battery chemistry: These batteries generally offer long cycle life and good thermal stability, though the complete product design still matters.
 Charging speed and adjustable charging limits: A high charging rate is convenient, but lowering it can reduce circuit demand when your equipment is running.
 Mains, solar and vehicle charging options: These provide useful flexibility during extended outages, travel or off-grid use.
 Manufacturer guidance for continuous use: Check whether the brand permits permanent pass-through operation and how it recommends maintaining the battery.
 Display, app monitoring or shutdown communication: Monitoring can help you track load and remaining runtime; USB communication may be essential for automatic PC shutdown.
 Before installation, measure your real load with a plug-in power meter. A computer labelled with a large maximum wattage may use far less during normal work, while a printer, heater or fridge can create unexpected peaks.
 Also consider ventilation and placement. Keep the station dry, away from heat and accessible enough to inspect. Do not connect it to household wiring or a wall socket through an improvised cable. A qualified electrician should install any fixed home-backup connection and transfer equipment.
 Best Portable Power Stations with UPS for 2026
 When choosing a portable power station for UPS use, transfer time, AC output, battery capacity and runtime matter more than capacity alone. The Anker SOLIX S2000 and C2000 Gen 2 combine substantial energy storage with backup capabilities, making them useful for keeping compatible computers, networking equipment and other electronics powered during outages.
 Anker SOLIX S2000
 The Anker SOLIX S2000 is well suited to users who want portable energy storage that can also provide backup for compatible electronics. Its ≤10 ms UPS switching is particularly relevant for this use, while its 2,010 Wh capacity offers considerably longer runtime potential than a typical small computer UPS.
 ≤10 ms UPS switching helps compatible equipment continue operating when mains power fails.
 2,010 Wh capacity provides extended backup for computers, routers and other essential electronics.
 1,500 W AC output allows several compatible devices to be powered simultaneously.
 LFP battery with up to 10,000 cycles supports frequent charging and standby use.
 Up to 400 W solar input provides another way to recharge during an extended outage.
 Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 Portable Power Station
 The Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 is a stronger option when higher output or longer runtime is required. Its 2,400 W rated output can accommodate demanding home-office equipment and other appliances, while expandable storage makes it useful when outages last longer than a conventional UPS battery can support.
 ≤10 ms UPS switching helps compatible equipment continue operating when mains power fails.
 2,400 W rated and 4,000 W peak output supports demanding computers and multiple connected devices.
 Expandable to 4 kWh with a BP2000 Gen 2 expansion battery for longer outage protection.
 Fast recharging reaches 80% in 45 minutes and 100% in 58 minutes with AC and solar fast charging.
 Only 9 W idle consumption helps reduce unnecessary battery use while equipment is on standby.
 Six recharge methods provide additional flexibility during prolonged power interruptions.
 Conclusion
 A portable power station can be used as a UPS when it has a genuine UPS, EPS or backup mode, fast enough transfer time and reliable pass-through charging. Pure sine wave output, adequate continuous wattage and sufficient usable capacity are also essential. These features make it useful for broadband equipment, computers, home offices and selected appliances during power cuts.
 The right choice depends on your priorities. A conventional UPS is usually simpler for short computer shutdowns, while an UPS portable power station offers longer runtime, portability and solar charging. Check the manual, measure your load and test the setup before trusting it with important equipment.
 FAQ
 Can you use a portable power station as a UPS?
 Yes, you can use a portable power station as a UPS when it specifically supports automatic backup or UPS mode. The station must remain connected to mains power, pass electricity through to your equipment and switch to its inverter during an outage.
 What is portable power station UPS mode?
 Portable power station UPS mode is a setting that allows the unit to supply connected equipment while mains power is available, then automatically use its internal battery when the mains fails. This is also described as EPS, backup mode or pass-through backup.
 Can I use a portable power station as a UPS for a PC?
 Yes, you can use a portable power station as a UPS for a PC if it provides pure sine wave output, adequate continuous wattage and a sufficiently short transfer time. A desktop computer with a high-performance graphics card may require substantial power, particularly during demanding tasks.
 Is a portable power station safe for a router, NAS or server?
 A portable power station is generally suitable for a router or NAS when it has pure sine wave output and an appropriate UPS transfer time. These devices often consume little power, so even a modest battery can provide several hours of runtime.
 How long will a portable power station run my equipment during a power cut?
 Runtime depends on usable watt-hours, inverter efficiency and the equipment’ s actual consumption. As a rough calculation, divide usable battery capacity by load in watts, then allow for conversion losses. For example, 800Wh divided by a 200W load suggests four hours before losses.

 UPS for a NAS - the Cable Matters More Than the Battery
 Quick answer
 A NAS does not need to ride out the outage. It needs two or three minutes to flush its writes, unmount its volumes and stop cleanly - so the data connection is the feature, not the runtime. Pick a pure sine unit with USB, confirm your NAS sees it, then pull the plug deliberately and watch it work.

 How many listings actually tell you the waveform

 The asymmetry is the finding. Pure sine is a selling point and gets printed; a stepped approximation is not and does not. So a silent listing is more likely to be the cheaper waveform than the better one, and we still do not claim to know which - we count it as unknown and tell you to check the datasheet.
 What the NAS actually does when the power goes
 Every NAS operating system worth running has the same three-stage response and it is worth knowing before you shop, because it tells you which specification to care about. Stage one: the UPS reports that mains has failed. Stage two: a countdown, either a fixed period you set or a wait until the UPS reports low battery. Stage three: the NAS stops services, unmounts its volumes and powers down cleanly.
 The whole sequence is a couple of minutes. It is not a strategy for staying online through an outage, and treating it as one is how people end up buying four times the battery they need. A NAS that shuts down cleanly at minute three has fully succeeded. A NAS with a two-hour battery and no data cable has fully failed, just later.
 Synology's implementation lives in Control Panel under Hardware and Power, and their own documentation describes the choice as either a custom delay or waiting until low battery, after which the unit enters Safe Mode. QNAP's QTS exposes the same shape under External Device, with two configurable responses to a power failure: power off after a set period, or enter auto-protection mode, which their documentation describes as stopping all services and unmounting all volumes to protect your data. TrueNAS runs its UPS service on Network UPS Tools and exposes master and slave modes so one machine can watch the UPS and the rest can watch that machine.
 The practical consequence: if you already run TrueNAS, or a Linux box, or anything else that can run NUT, then the vendor compatibility list is much less binding than it looks, because NUT talks to a very large number of units directly.
 NUT, and why we link it instead of reproducing it
 Network UPS Tools is the open-source project that most of this ecosystem quietly rests on. In the project's own words its goal is "to provide support for Power Devices, such as Uninterruptible Power Supplies, Power Distribution Units, Automatic Transfer Switches, Power Supply Units and Solar Controllers", offering a common protocol and set of tools across manufacturers' incompatible ones. It is GPL licensed.
 Its hardware compatibility list is the reference document for this question. At the date we read it, it recorded at least 199 manufacturers and 1,436 device models as known compatible - a very different number from any single NAS vendor's tested list.
 We link that list rather than reproducing it, and the reason is a rule we apply generally: a stale copy of somebody else's compatibility list is worse than a link to the live one. It is maintained upstream, it changes, and a reader who checks our snapshot from months ago and finds their model missing has been actively misled by us. Go to the source: it is the single most useful page on this subject and it is not ours.
 The practical route for most people is simpler than the list suggests. Plug the unit into the NAS by USB, open the UPS settings, and see whether the machine reports a battery. Most modern units present themselves through a generic HID power-device interface and are recognised without any configuration at all. If it appears, you are done. If it does not, the compatibility list is where to look next.
 Sizing for a NAS, and the honest gap in it
 The sizing method is the one on the hub page and it comes from Synology rather than from us: total the real wattage of everything on the UPS, then divide by the unit's output power factor to get the output rating you need. Synology's worked example puts a 650 W total against a 70% power factor and arrives at 928.5 W.
 What we cannot give you is the first number. This site publishes no per-device wattage - not for a four-bay NAS, not for an eight-bay, not for a switch - because we have not fetched and logged a maker datasheet for each machine, and a wattage attributed to a typical device of that shape is not a citation. Your NAS publishes its own figure. On Synology's spec pages it sits under power consumption, usually with two values, one for access and one for hibernation, and a note about the drive configuration it was measured with. That last part matters: the figure moves with how many drives you have fitted, because most of the draw is spinning platters, not the chassis.
 Two additions people forget. Drives spinning up simultaneously at power-on draw substantially more than they do at idle, so a unit sized exactly to the running figure has no headroom for a restart. And the network switch between the NAS and everything else needs to be on the same UPS, or the NAS survives the outage in perfect isolation and nobody can reach it.
 What our own catalogue can tell you is what is on the shelf at each VA band and what real power those units claim - that table is on the hub, it is a measurement of our inventory, and it is labelled as one rather than dressed up as a recommendation about your hardware.
 One UPS, several machines
 The common homelab shape is one UPS carrying a NAS, a switch, and one or two other machines, and the question is how the machines that do not hold the USB cable find out about the outage.
 All three ecosystems solve it the same way, with different names. Synology's compatibility page states it plainly: any model on their list can extend UPS service to a second Synology product using Network UPS Server, where the first machine connects by USB and relays the information to clients on the local network. QNAP exposes network UPS master and slave modes. TrueNAS calls it master and slave and, being NUT underneath, will happily act as either against a non-TrueNAS peer.
 Because they are all speaking the same underlying protocol, mixed environments generally work: a TrueNAS box holding the cable can signal a Linux machine running NUT, and a Synology acting as server can be watched by another Synology. What is not guaranteed is any particular cross-vendor pairing, and we are not going to assert one we have not tested.
 Synology adds one hardware caveat worth repeating because it catches people: connect the USB device directly to a USB port on the product. Connecting through a hub is not supported. If your NAS is behind a hub for want of ports, that is the first thing to eliminate when it fails to see the UPS.
 Test it, because nobody else will
 This is the step that gets skipped and it is the only one that proves the purchase worked. The instruction is not ours - it is on Synology's own compatibility page, attached to the tested list: the UPS power-off function varies by brand and model, so simulate a power outage to ensure the function performs as expected.
 Do it deliberately, on a day when nothing is at stake, with nothing important being written. Pull the mains plug on the UPS - not the switch, the plug - and watch. The NAS should log the loss within seconds, count down, and shut down. Then restore power and confirm it comes back up and remounts cleanly.
 Repeat it after any change to the chain: a new UPS battery, a firmware update on either device, moving the cable to a different port. And repeat it when the battery is around three years old, because a battery that has aged out will still let the NAS see the UPS and report a healthy state right up until the moment it is asked to actually supply power.
 A shutdown chain that has never been tested is a shutdown chain you are guessing about, and the outage is a bad time to find out that the guess was wrong.
 Where to go next
 The UPS hub has the waveform rule and the sizing method in full · Rackmount units if the NAS lives in a rack · NAS devices , the DS925+ and drive compatibility by machine cover the other end of the cable · NAS drives and filling a NAS are the array itself · enclosures share the outlet and want counting into the load.
 Frequently asked questions
 Does my UPS have to be on Synology's compatibility list? No, and the list is narrower than most readers assume. It is category-level rather than per-machine, and a large share of the tested units are regional SKUs built for other mains supplies - Synology lists BR1500MS-TW where the US shelf carries BR1500MS2. Not listed means Synology has not tested that exact SKU; it is not a compatibility verdict. Most modern units present a generic HID power-device interface over USB and are recognised without configuration.
 How much runtime does a NAS need? Minutes, not hours. The job is to notice the outage, stop services, unmount volumes and power down cleanly, which takes a couple of minutes on a normal array. Buying a much larger battery to keep serving files through an outage is a different and much more expensive goal, and it only works if the network switch and everything else in the path are on the same protection.
 Can one UPS shut down more than one machine? Yes. One machine holds the USB cable and relays the state to the others over the network. Synology calls it Network UPS Server, QNAP calls it network UPS master and slave, and TrueNAS calls it master and slave. All three are speaking Network UPS Tools underneath, which is why mixed setups usually work - though we do not assert any specific cross-vendor pairing we have not tested.
 Can I plug the UPS into my NAS through a USB hub? Synology's own guidance says no - connect USB devices directly to a USB port on the Synology product, because connecting via a hub is not supported. If a NAS cannot see a UPS that is otherwise working, a hub in the path is the first thing to eliminate.
 What is NUT and do I need it? Network UPS Tools is the open-source project that provides a common protocol for monitoring power devices across manufacturers, licensed under the GPL. You do not install it on a Synology or QNAP - it is already underneath the vendor's UPS feature. You do use it directly on TrueNAS, Linux and BSD machines. Its hardware compatibility list recorded at least 199 manufacturers and 1,436 models at the date we read it, which is a far broader set than any single NAS vendor's tested list.
 How do I know the shutdown actually works? Test it, and take the instruction from the vendor rather than from us: Synology's compatibility page says the power-off function varies by brand and model and to simulate a power outage to ensure it performs as expected. Pull the mains plug deliberately, on a quiet day, and watch the NAS notice, count down and stop. Repeat after any firmware or hardware change, and again when the battery is a few years old.
 Sources
 Specification claims on this page were checked against the pages below on 4 August 2026 . Where a widely-repeated figure did not survive that check, we report what the source says now and say so in the text rather than repeating the familiar number.
 CyberPower Systems - Active PFC Compatibility (glossary) ( cyberpowersystems.com , 2026-08-20 ) Used for: the maker's own definition, quoted verbatim on our pages: Active PFC compatibility is "a feature of UPS systems that delivers sine wave output to prevent unexpected shutdowns or component stress for connected devices with Active PFC power supplies." This is the source for the spec-gate framing - the failure mode named by the maker is an unexpected shutdown, which is precisely the event a UPS was bought to prevent.
 Synology Inc. - How do I choose a suitable UPS? (Knowledge Center) ( kb.synology.com , 2026-08-20 ) Used for: the sizing method used on these pages, quoted rather than paraphrased: "Output power = Total wattage of your devices / Output power factor of a UPS", with Synology's own worked example dividing a 650 W load by a 70% power factor to reach 928.5 W. Also the VA-versus-watts caveat in the vendor's own words: "Different manufacturers have different volt-ampere (VA) ratings based on the performance of their UPS. To determine the total power (W) that the UPS can support, we recommend consulting the manufacturer's product manual." Article last updated 1 April 2024.
 Synology Inc. - Products Compatibility List - UPS, filtered to tested by Synology ( synology.com , 2026-08-20 ) Used for: the full tested list, captured in a rendered browser session: 79 entries, 73 UPS units and 6 management cards or protocol adapters. Also the vendor's own two operational notes, which we quote rather than restate: that any listed model can extend UPS service to a second Synology product over the network, and that "The UPS power-off function varies by brand and model. Please simulate a power outage to ensure the function performs as expected." The list is CATEGORY-level: it does not filter per machine.
 QNAP Systems - Configuring the UPS settings, QTS 5.2.x ( docs.qnap.com , 2026-08-20 ) Used for: that QTS supports three connection modes - USB cable, SNMP over the network, and network UPS slave against another machine acting as the server - and the two configurable responses to a power failure: powering off after a set period, or entering auto-protection mode, which stops services and unmounts volumes.
 Network UPS Tools project - Network UPS Tools (NUT) - project overview and hardware compatibility list ( networkupstools.org , 2026-08-20 ) Used for: the project's own description of its scope - "to provide support for Power Devices, such as Uninterruptible Power Supplies, Power Distribution Units, Automatic Transfer Switches, Power Supply Units and Solar Controllers" - its GPL licence, and the size of its hardware compatibility list at the date read: at least 199 manufacturers and 1,436 device models. We link this list; we do not reproduce it. It is maintained upstream, it changes, and a stale copy of somebody else's compatibility list is worse than a link to the live one.

( se.com , 2026-08-20 ) Used for: the three-to-five-year expected service life of the sealed lead-acid battery in a typical APC UPS, and that operating temperature is the dominant factor in shortening it. The replacement-cartridge prices quoted on our pages are described as reported figures, not as our measurement - we do not track UPS battery prices.

 For a NAS with local USB shutdown , start with the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD, current a revision : sine-wave output, six battery-backed outlets and USB HID management. Prefer APC? Choose BR1500MS2 for the pure-sine alternative, or SMC1500C when you need eight battery-backed outlets; the selected SMC offer includes USB storage.

 The new APC rows use the maker’s BR1500MS2 , BX1500M and SMC1500C sheets. Compare W/VA, waveform, outlet count and USB management separately, then choose runtime for your measured load.
 Best UPS for a NAS: pure sine plus a real USB data port
 A NAS UPS has two jobs: keep the disks powered through the interruption, then tell the NAS when it is time to stop. Buy the shutdown path as well as the battery. A front-panel USB charging socket cannot deliver that message.
 For a new NAS or server purchase, start with the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD’s current a revision . It combines sine-wave output, six battery-backed outlets and USB HID management. CyberPower explicitly lists active-PFC power-supply compatibility . The APC BR1500MS2 is the pure-sine APC alternative, also with six battery-backed outlets; the SMC1500C gives you eight.
 The BX1500M is the contrast pick , with what APC calls a “stepped approximation to a sinewave.” Choose it only when that waveform meets your equipment’s power-supply requirements. Sine-wave output is the simpler starting choice for a new active-PFC NAS/server build; the BX’s similar VA/W label does not make its output identical to the BR1500MS2’s.
 That is different from topology. These APC models and the CyberPower are line-interactive units, not zero-transfer-time online UPSs. Waveform, transfer, runtime and USB communication are separate specifications. Our power-station-as-UPS guide shows why a larger portable battery needs the same questions answered.

 Which USB port—and which cable?
 Use the UPS’s management connection and a matching data cable. On the BR1500MS2, the front USB-A/USB-C charging ports are separate from UPS communication. On the SMC1500C, SmartConnect Ethernet is cloud monitoring ; local USB management is a separate connection. Its selected Amazon offer is a tower UPS bundled with 16 GB USB storage . The flash drive is a bundle extra, not the UPS data connection.
 GOLDENMATE’s six-outlet 600VA maker page describes simulated-sine output and PC communication. The lithium battery is interesting, but choose one of the documented driver routes above for this NAS job until a matching 600VA NUT record is available. Do not substitute its five-outlet wall-mount sibling or a 1000VA driver report.
 Set up USB shutdown in TrueNAS, Unraid or Synology
 Start by plugging the NAS into a battery-backed outlet , then connect the management cable directly to the machine that will monitor the UPS. Keep that USB device available to the host instead of passing it into a VM that should shut down first.
 TrueNAS: the 25.10 UPS service guide uses NUT. Open System → Services , edit UPS , select the driver and USB device that match the NUT record, then set the shutdown policy. Save the configuration and start the service. The NUT usbhid-ups manual explains the USB driver; a basic standalone NUT configuration uses driver = usbhid-ups and port = auto .
 Unraid: open Settings → UPS Settings for its built-in UPS support. That service uses apcupsd , not NUT. The Unraid UPS guidance covers USB connection and shutdown thresholds. If you choose the NUT plugin instead, follow the NUT project’s Unraid setup : set Start APC UPS daemon → No , apply the change, then configure NUT. One service should own the USB UPS, not two competing daemons.
 Synology DSM: open Control Panel → Hardware & Power → UPS , enable UPS support and select USB UPS . Choose the time before Standby Mode as described in Synology’s USB UPS instructions . Standby Mode stops services and unmounts volumes; build that step into the shutdown plan rather than expecting the NAS to run until the battery is flat.
 Test the boring bit before the first outage
 Confirm live status. With mains available, the NAS should report the UPS and battery state. Look for battery charge and mains/battery status in the NAS interface.
 Choose shutdown reserve. Allow time for applications, VMs and storage to stop, plus a margin for an ageing battery. The UPS sizing guide gives you the worksheet.
 Run a controlled power-loss test. Follow the UPS maker’s procedure, with a current backup and nonessential work first. Confirm that the NAS sees battery operation and completes its configured shutdown before power runs out.
 Restore input and check recovery. Observe the UPS output, NAS restart behavior and storage status. If another machine supplies network UPS status, keep the network path powered until shutdown finishes.
 Choosing the NAS too? Our UGREEN DXP2800 vs Synology DS225+ comparison separates media and backup roles. Give whichever you choose enough time to close its work cleanly.
 Modest single-box load: APC
 Choose the APC for the modest single-box case. Its six battery-backed outlets are enough for a single host and a deliberately small set of shutdown dependencies, provided their combined W and VA budgets fit.
 For scale, the existing UPS-sizing worksheet chooses a 240 W host at 0.96 power factor . That is 250 VA ; applying the worksheet’s chosen 25% growth allowance to that host alone gives 300 W / 312.5 VA . Those are illustrative inputs, not typical consumption figures. They fit the APC’s ratings, leaving runtime as the next decision.
 Small-rack pick: CyberPower
 For a host, switch and NAS, start with the CyberPower , provided six battery-backed outlets cover the equipment that must survive the outage. Its other six outlets are surge-only: they do not keep a switch or shutdown controller running on battery.
 The sizing guide’s complete fictional rack adds a 30 W / 50 VA network load and 10 W / 20 VA controller to the host. Total demand is 280 W / 320 VA , or 350 W / 400 VA after the chosen growth allowance. All seven selected models clear that capacity worksheet. Choose between them using outlet requirements, runtime evidence, management support and physical fit rather than treating the largest VA label as necessary.
 CyberPower’s manual recommends keeping load below 80% of rated capacity for optimal performance. For the current version, keep the design below 800 W and 1,200 VA . The illustrative rack clears both; use the model’s runtime information to plan minutes on battery.
 Check the delivered revision carefully. Amazon’s model field identifies CP1500PFCLCDA , matching the vendor’s CP1500PFCLCDa specifications . Older CP1500PFCLCD records describe 900 W hardware. Do not apply the current 1,000 W limit or replacement-battery choice to an older unit by name alone.
 When eight Eaton battery outlets matter
 Buy the 5SC1000 when eight direct battery-backed outlets solve a real connection problem and 700 W / 1,000 VA covers your planned load. Buy the 5SC1500 when that outlet arrangement matters and you need the higher 1,080 W / 1,440 VA capacity. Both have USB HID data and a separate serial connection; the serial RJ45 connector is not an Ethernet management interface.
 Choose the Eaton when eight battery-backed outlets solve the connection requirement. Count devices that genuinely need battery power and check their plug spacing.
 Eaton documents front-access battery replacement. Keep access and ventilation clear when choosing a shelf; fitting the cabinet’s footprint is not enough if you cannot service the battery. Follow the exact replacement procedure and select the supported pack rather than assuming every battery that physically fits is suitable.
 For a two-GPU inference box, measure the whole protected load
 The CyberPower is the first capacity candidate , not an automatic match for two GPUs. A PSU output-capacity label and GPU telemetry do not give the protected equipment’s AC W/VA demand. Include the rest of the host and any switch or storage dependency needed for shutdown. The plug-in meter comparison helps choose the measurement tool.
 For a buying example, choose an already-planned budget of 700 W / 800 VA . This is an arbitrary worksheet case, not a measured or typical two-GPU system. It fits the current CyberPower’s below-80% recommendation. The 5SC1500 also clears both nameplate limits and provides eight battery-backed outlets. The 5SC1000 would sit at its watt ceiling; choose a model with room for the actual design instead.
 If the measured load and chosen reserve exceed the candidate’s limits, reduce the protected load or select a different UPS. Select runtime separately from output capacity.
 Read the revision-specific NUT records
 Use the management data connection , not the front charging ports. The APC BR1000MS NUT report identifies usbhid-ups and explicitly leaves its shutdown sequence untested. The CyberPower DDL covers an older 900 W unit; NUT’s CyberPower driver source separately names CP1500PFCLCDa handling. The compatibility list supplies 5SC-family USB evidence for Eaton, not an exact 5SC1000/1500 shutdown test.
 During the shutdown test, follow the complete sequence: status reporting, the shutdown decision, host halt, UPS output behavior and restart. Keep required communication equipment powered until the host has finished.
 Give the battery box proper support as well as suitable power. Our small rack and shelf guide separates tower-UPS shelving from four-post rack equipment, with depth, load and cable-space checks.
 Buy enough time, not just enough watts
 Use the sizing guide to define the protected load, runtime target and shutdown order. Check the exact model’s runtime information at that load, then validate the complete design under stated battery and charge conditions. Do not turn VA or battery watt-hours into guaranteed minutes.
 Choose CyberPower for the pure-sine NAS/rack starting point, BR1500MS2 for the APC alternative, and SMC1500C or Eaton when eight battery outlets matter . Keep BR1000MS for the modest single box; choose BX1500M only for equipment that accepts stepped sine. The useful UPS fits the load and finishes the shutdown you planned.
 Need longer networking runtime or a battery you can take with you? Our portable power station as a UPS guide compares transfer times, router runtime and the RIVER 3 Max’s USB shutdown route.
 For a router and ONT that can use DC backup directly, our DC mini UPS guide walks through voltage range, polarity, plug fit and runtime estimates before you choose a pack.
